clue.text: Musketeer is a bad shot

indicators.note: a bad shot goes astray, so these letters are knocked out of their order

explanation.surface: Someone sneers that one of Dumas's swordsmen can't aim straight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bad' sits inside its fodder and rearranges A + SHOT; 'is' links the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: One of the three heroes of Dumas's novel The Three Musketeers, alongside Porthos and Aramis.

clue.text: Publican with no end of trade

indicators.note: with no means the following word is taken out of the publican's job title

parts.note: a bartender serves drinks, as a publican does
taken as written

explanation.surface: A pub landlord finds business never stops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with no' takes END out of BARTENDER; 'end' is the very letters removed, not an instruction to cut the last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To barter is to trade goods by exchange rather than for money; both are verbs of dealing.

clue.text: Public company that could be mine

parts.note: public means open to all
the company of a play is its cast

explanation.surface: A firm going public might turn out to be one's own.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mine' is the pit, not the possessive: an opencast mine is worked from the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Opencast describes a mine dug from the surface rather than by shafts, so the word fits what could be a kind of mine.

clue.text: Sort of study carried out by bathyscope?

definitions.text: Sort of study carried out by bathyscope?

parts.words: Sort of study carried out by bathyscope?
parts.note: a deep-sea diving vessel literally works far down in the ocean, which describes a thorough kind of study

explanation.surface: Asking what research a deep-sea submersible does.
explanation.definitionFit: A thorough study is described by this phrase, and a bathyscope literally operates far down underwater.

clue.text: It's to do with the pursuit of game, naturally

definitions.text: It's to do with the pursuit of game
definitions.meaning: coursing is hunting hares with dogs, so the phrase can mean relating to coursing
naturally means certainly, as might be expected

explanation.surface: Hunting game is described as only natural.
explanation.definitionFit: Coursing is chasing hares with greyhounds, so the phrase read literally concerns it; as an idiom it means certainly or obviously.

clue.text: Heavenly organisation elects one for a student

indicators.note: organisation of the letters means arranging them into a new order

parts.note: the Roman numeral I is one
L is a learner, shown on a learner driver's plate

explanation.surface: A body of heavenly beings votes to admit someone as a pupil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'organisation' rearranges ELECTS + I + A + L; 'for' is a link word. L for learner is from the L-plate on British learner drivers' cars.
explanation.definitionFit: Celestial means of the sky or heaven, a synonym of heavenly.

clue.text: Very strong sticking-plaster

definitions.meaning: burly and powerful, as a big healthy person is
adhesive bandage material sold in strips

explanation.definitionFit: A strapping lad is big and sturdy; strapping is also the material used for binding wounds, such as adhesive plaster.

clue.text: Frequently expressed as decimal

definitions.meaning: decimal counting is in tens, so a decimal number is expressed in terms ...

explanation.surface: A number keeps being written as a decimal.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition splits the answer into two words: decimal means 'of ten'.
explanation.definitionFit: Often means many times, like frequently; split in two it says 'of ten', which is what decimal means.

clue.text: Spoken of curtailed ethic

indicators.note: curtailed means cut short, here losing the opening letter of the word for ethic

parts.note: an ethic is a moral principle, a moral

explanation.surface: Someone talks about a principle that has been cut back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'curtailed' strictly means losing the last letter; here the setter cuts the first, M, from MORAL. 'of' links.
explanation.definitionFit: Oral means uttered by mouth rather than written, the same as spoken.

clue.text: Don't give up getting the unit back in shape

indicators.note: in means the reversed word sits inside the word for a shape

parts.note: a cone is a solid geometric shape

indicators.note: back means the word unit is read in the opposite direction

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Encouragement to keep at it while getting a squad back into form.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns the word unit round and 'in' sets it inside a geometric solid; 'shape' looks like getting fit, but it names the solid. 'getting the' links.
explanation.definitionFit: To continue is to carry on, the opposite of giving up.

clue.text: Troublemaker returns to Brazil city square first

parts.note: Rio de Janeiro is the famous Brazilian city
a T-square is a drawing tool, so square gives T
read as RE turns, the word re (about) turned round gives ER

explanation.surface: A rabble-rouser goes back to Rio, heading first to the plaza.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returns' is split as RE + turns: RE reversed gives ER. 'square first' says T comes before ER; 'to' links.
explanation.definitionFit: A rioter takes part in a violent public disturbance, a kind of troublemaker.

clue.text: Article about a piece of land

parts.note: a is the indefinite article
re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: A newspaper article concerns a plot of ground.
explanation.definitionFit: An area is an expanse of ground, a region or tract.

clue.text: Permit strange to relate

indicators.note: strange signals the letters of the words are made unfamiliar by rearranging them

explanation.surface: Someone allows that a story is odd to tell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strange' rearranges TO RELATE.
explanation.definitionFit: To tolerate is to allow or put up with, a synonym of permit as a verb.

clue.text: Frank gets contract with unlimited resources

parts.note: frank means open and candid
to purse the lips is to contract them

explanation.surface: Someone called Frank signs a deal backed by bottomless funds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Frank' looks like a name but is the adjective; 'contract' is a verb, as in pursing the lips. 'gets' and 'with' link.
explanation.definitionFit: Having an open purse means money is freely available, so it stands for limitless funds.

clue.text: Ring through at one point for work

parts.note: a ring is round like the letter O
per means through or by means of
taken as written
E, east, is one point of the compass

explanation.surface: A telephone instruction to put a call through to a workplace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To operate a machine is to work it, and both verbs also mean to function.

clue.text: Criminal set?

definitions.meaning: a fence who handles stolen goods
a radio or television set picks up broadcasts

explanation.surface: Asking whether a crook is a setup.
explanation.definitionFit: A receiver is a fence, one who handles stolen property, and also a radio or TV apparatus that picks up signals.

clue.text: Reserve of strength in a football team!

definitions.meaning: a store of weapons or resources

explanation.surface: A football side has plenty of strength in hand.
explanation.definitionFit: An arsenal is a stockpile of weapons or resources; Arsenal is also a famous north London football club.

clue.text: Possibly press one for an answer

indicators.note: possibly means the letters could be arranged differently

explanation.surface: An automated phone menu telling the caller which key to hit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' rearranges PRESS ONE; 'for an' links.
explanation.definitionFit: A response is a reply, the same as an answer.

clue.text: Tried writing to the editor

parts.note: an essay is a piece of writing

explanation.surface: Someone attempted to write a letter to the paper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to the' links the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To essay something is to attempt it, so essayed means attempted.

clue.text: Thieves commonly said to take ladies' underwear

indicators.note: said means the word is spoken, so its sound counts rather than its spelling

parts.note: to nick is British slang for to steal, so thieves are nickers in common speech

explanation.surface: Burglars are reported to pinch women's lingerie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'commonly' marks the slang: in Britain 'nick' means steal. 'to take' links.
explanation.definitionFit: Knickers are women's pants, an item of lingerie in British English.

clue.text: Provides encouragement for poaching, perhaps

definitions.meaning: to urge someone on, as in egging on
food that can be poached in simmering water, among other ways of cooking

explanation.surface: Someone is urging on game-stealing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'poaching' suggests illegal hunting, but it is the cooking method.
explanation.definitionFit: To egg someone on is to urge them; and hens' produce is cooked by poaching, frying or boiling.

clue.text: Such puddings make a girl fat in the end

parts.note: Sue is a girl's name

indicators.note: in the end picks only the closing letter of the word fat

explanation.surface: Stodgy puddings eventually make a young woman put on weight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'make' links. Suet pudding is a heavy British dish made with beef or mutton fat.
explanation.definitionFit: Suet puddings are a traditional British stodgy dessert or savoury dish, so the answer names that kind of pudding.

clue.text: Noted national property

parts.note: E is a musical note, so the word gives a note
the state is the nation, as in state-owned

explanation.surface: A famous property held by the nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Noted' looks like 'famous' but supplies the note E; 'national' gives STATE, as in a state-run industry.
explanation.definitionFit: An estate is land or possessions held by someone, a kind of property.

clue.text: Moving arm up and down

indicators.note: up and down means the letters read the same going up or down this down entry

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: An arm that swings back and forth.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry the word reads the same upwards and downwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A rotor is the turning part of a machine, such as a helicopter blade, a revolving arm.

clue.text: Copper band used for healing

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
a ring is a band, as worn on a finger

explanation.surface: A copper bracelet worn as a remedy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'used for' links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Curing is making well, the same as healing.

clue.text: Notice work getting into shape for a take-over

parts.note: an ad is a notice or advertisement
op is short for opus, a work

indicators.note: getting into shape means the letters are rearranged into a new form

explanation.surface: An advertisement prompts a fitness drive ahead of a corporate takeover.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shape' rearranges INTO to TION; 'getting' links, and 'for a' links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Adoption is taking something over as one's own, such as a child or a policy.

clue.text: He splits a couple of poles made of wood

indicators.note: splits means the word He breaks into the middle of the poles

parts.note: S and N are the south and north poles
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man splits two posts made of timber.
explanation.walkthrough: 'splits' puts HE between S and N.
explanation.definitionFit: Ashen can describe something crafted from ash timber.

clue.text: Excitement as tension explodes

indicators.note: explodes means the letters are blown apart and reassembled

explanation.surface: Tension bursts, causing a thrill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'explodes' rearranges AS TENSION.
explanation.definitionFit: A sensation is a stir of public excitement or interest.
